new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is free (distinctive): every polysyllabic word has one stressed syllable whose position is fixed neither by syllable phonetics nor by distance from a word edge but by the accentual value of the word's morphemes (strong vs weak stems, strong vs weak endings) plus 'attractive' endings that pull stress off a preceding non-acuted syllable (the penultimate-syllable rule = de Saussure-Fortunatov law); nominals fall into four accentuation classes diagnosed by dative/accusative plural. Long stressed syllables additionally carry one of two tonemes (acute = sharp falling, circumflex = smooth rising); short stressed syllables carry stress only (grave = stress mark, not a toneme); toneme contrasts are neutralised in unstressed syllables. Stress is phonetically of a 'mixed type' (loudness, pitch, some length). Clitics are unstressed; monosyllables pattern with stressed syllables.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §6.3: a lower-degree (secondary) stress may occur, especially in western dialects, most often on the second post-tonic syllable (mainly the penult) of a longer word (mókytojas, pùskepalis); a phonological secondary stress is possible in some rural dialects and idiolects of the standard ((tu) mýli vs (jis) mýli type pairs).
new_statements.exceptions: Some dialects restrict the freedom of stress (§6.1); toneme neutralisation in final syllables has exceptions (datives in -m(s), adverbs pusiaũ, visái, pronouns jóks, tóks, interjections, §6.9); in Samogitian dialects acute is the unmarked toneme and occurs post-tonically (§6.10); attractive endings override stem stress only after a non-acuted syllable (§2.3).
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Lithuanian (bendrinė kalba); Tanaka 1974 explicitly 'Standard Lithuanian'; Vidžiūnas 1996 concerns the East-Prussian (Lithuania Minor) written tradition of the 17th-19th c; Frings 1934 compares the Rhenish (German dialect) and Lithuanian tonal accents.

tone_statements.translation: §41. In some languages stressed syllables are not pronounced uniformly; they differ in priegaidė [syllable accent] (as noted in §3, terms vary in English, the prevailing one is pitch-accent) - a modulation of the syllable's pronunciation able to distinguish otherwise identical words or forms, e.g. lénkė and leñkė, téisė and teĩsė. In Standard Lithuanian two accents of long stressed syllables are distinguished: tvirtapradė (acute) and tvirtagalė (circumflex). ... The acute differs from the circumflex by sharply falling intensity and fundamental frequency and by shorter duration.

Sutariama, kad tokia opozicija egzistuoja tiek standartinėje kalboje, tiek tarmėse (Girdenis 2003, 268–277; DLKG 2005, 39; Pakerys 2003, 219–223; Stundžia 2014, 24–27 ...). ... tone_statements.translation: Both Lithuanian tonemes - the circumflex and the acute - form a phonological opposition (contrast) in stressed position; their contrast performs a distinctive function - it distinguishes words and their forms. It is agreed that such an opposition exists both in the standard language and in the dialects (Girdenis 2003 ...). ... The position of the tonemes, compared e.g. with the members of the vowel or consonant systems, is special: the whole inventory of phonological tones consists of only two members.

Trys skiemenį sudarančių garsų tipai formuoja iš esmės (fonetiškai ir fonologiškai) skirtingus priegaidžių variantus. Jie yra 1) dvigarsiuose a, e + l, m, n, r ir dvibalsiuose ai, au, ei (plg. káltas – kal̃tas, mérkti – mer̃.kti, á.ušta – aũ.šta ...), 2) dvigarsiuose i, u + l, m, n, r ir dvibalsyje ui ..., ir 3) ilguosiuose balsiuose ... bei sutaptiniuose dvibalsiuose ie, uo (týrė – tỹrė, ... kóšė – kõšė, líeknas – liẽknas).
tone_statements.translation: In Lithuanian there is phonologically an opposition of two syllable accents - 'firm-beginning' and 'firm-end' (acute and circumflex) - in long stressed syllables. Three types of syllable-forming sounds produce essentially (phonetically and phonologically) different variants of the accents. They are 1) in the mixed diphthongs a, e + l, m, n, r and the diphthongs ai, au, ei (cf. káltas - kal̃tas, mérkti - mer̃.kti, á.ušta - aũ.šta ...), 2) in the mixed diphthongs i, u + l, m, n, r and the diphthong ui ..., and 3) in long vowels ... and the gliding diphthongs ie, uo (týrė - tỹrė, ... kóšė - kõšė, líeknas - liẽknas).

tone_statements.quote: Stress in the Lithuanian language is FREE, i.e. it can occur on any syllable of a word: the ultimate, the penultimate, the first and any other. Alongside its universal CULMINATIVE function, which is fulfilled by stresses of all types, this type of stress primarily performs a DISTINCTIVE function because the place of a word stress can distinguish lexical and grammatical meanings of words [...] (p. 431). In longer words with at least three syllables, alongside the PRIMARY stress, one or several SECONDARY stresses can be optionally realized (p. 432). Two phonological pitch accents exist in Standard Lithuanian and all its dialects, namely THE ACUTE ACCENT [...] and THE CIRCUMFLEX ACCENT [...], which contrast in stressed long syllables, those containing long vowels, diphthongs and VR-type diphthongoid sequences (p. 434).

tone_statements.quote: Most modern sources ascribe the plural tėvaĩ to AP4, which implies oxytone stress and non-acute stem vowel (*tėṽ-), i. e. métatonie douce. [...] Oxytone stress (tėvùs) is signaled as regular in Modern Lithuanian by most reference works, regardless of the meaning (‘fathers’ or ‘parents’); it indicates AP4. sources.quote: Stress in the Lithuanian language is FREE, i.e. it can occur on any syllable of a word: the ultimate, the penultimate, the first and any other. sources.citation: Gleim, Daniel, Gereon Müller, Mariia Privizentseva & Sören E. Tebay. 2022. Reflexes of exponent movement in inflectional morphology: A study in Harmonic Serialism. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 41: 103-158. doi:10.1007/s11049-022-09543-4
sources.quote: Phonological words in Lithuanian have one main pitch accent. Accent can be assigned to any mora (μ) in a word; and there can be up to two moras in the rhyme of a syllable. Depending on where the mora ending up with the main accent is located in a syllable, this produces what Leskien (1919) calls falling vs. rising—or gestoßene ('pushed') vs. geschleifte ('dragged')—accents [...] Any morphological exponent can bear an inherent lexical accent. Normally, if a stem and an inflectional exponent are both pre-specified for accent, it is the accent on the stem that prevails; i.e., the leftmost accent wins (the Basic Accentuation Principle; cf. Halle and Vergnaud 1987). sources.quote: Lithuanian is a language in which not only phonetic ingredients of a sound, but also prosodic features are phonologically distinctive. There are found the following prosodic oppositions in it: according to the position of stress, according to the character of stress (falling and rising), and according to the quantity of both stressed and unstressed syllables. Both falling and rising stress can characterize any stressed long syllable. But this is characteristic not of all the Lithuanian dialects. [...] Stress in the North-east Aukštaičiai dialects is retracted from the last on to the preceding syllable. [...] In the Žemaičiai dialect dynamic word-stress combines with musical syllable-stress and with well developed phonetic syllable-stress. Intonations are opposed here as high (acute) — low (circumflex).

sources.note: States the Lithuanian prosodic oppositions (stress place, falling vs rising accent, quantity) and their dialectal distribution, including stress retraction in North-east Aukštaitian.

tone.translation: §41. In some languages stressed syllables are not pronounced uniformly; they differ in priegaidė [syllable accent] (as noted in §3, terms vary in English, the prevailing one is pitch-accent) - a modulation of the syllable's pronunciation able to distinguish otherwise identical words or forms, e.g. lénkė and leñkė, téisė and teĩsė.
